text:
Interviewer: This is a United States Holocaust Memorial Museum interview with Floor Miller, on October 15th, 2010, conducted by Jackie Smith in Fort Lee, New Jersey. Mrs. Miller, thank you very much for agreeing to be interviewed today.
Interviewee: You’re welcome.
Interviewer: I’d like to begin our interview with some idea about your family, your young — your youth, your childhood, who your parents were. So I’ll se — ask those types of questions. Can you tell me when were you born, and what your name at birth was?
Interviewee: March 2nd, 1913, and my name was Floor Davids.
Interviewer: Floor Davids.
Interviewee: Yeah.
Interviewer: And where were you born?
Interviewee: In Schlüchtern, in Germany.
Interviewer: Schlüchtern? Where is Schlüchtern?
Interviewee: Schlüchtern is — Schlüchtern, Frankfurt and Fulda.
Interviewer: Ah, it’s between Frankfurt am Main and Fulda?
Interviewee: Yeah.
Interviewer: So you were kind of in central Germany. Is that Hessen?
Interviewee: Yes, yeah.
Interviewer: Is that the land of Hessen?
Interviewee: It’s Hessen, Hessen.
Interviewer: Okay. Is Schlüchtern a village or a town?
Interviewee: A small town.
Interviewer: A small town. Who were your parents?
Interviewee: Hans — the names?
Interviewer: Yeah, the names.
Interviewee: Hans and Elsje Davids.
Interviewer: Hans and Elsje?
Interviewee: Davids.
Interviewer: And is Elsje spelled e-l-s-j-e?
Interviewee: Yeah.
Interviewer: Okay. Davids. Would you remember about when they were born?
Interviewee: *** but, hell, I had it in my hand the other day.
Interviewee: A — 1881.
Interviewer: Oh, so they were young parents, actually. Or maybe not, maybe 20 - 30 years old. Hans was born in?
Interviewee: He was in — was he — wait a minute.
Interviewee: That’s Elsje.
Interviewee: Davids.
Interviewee: This is Elsje, eight — 1883.
Interviewee: Wait a — my mother —
Interviewee: No, 1886.
Interviewee: My mother was born in nine — in 1886.
Interviewer: Okay, and your father?
Interviewee: 1881.
Interviewer: Okay. Are you the only child in the family?
Interviewee: I had a brother, he passed away.
Interviewer: Was he older or younger?
Interviewee: He was a year younger.
Interviewer: And what was his name?
Interviewee: Ernst Davids.
Interviewer: Ernst Davids, okay. And what was your father — what was your father’s profession? What did he do to make a living?
Interviewee: He was a — a — how — how do you call it, a salesman.
Interviewer: He was a salesman?
Interviewee: Y-Yeah. He’s — he was in business himself.
Interviewer: In what way? Did he have a store, or did he —
Interviewee: We had a store in the house, yes.
Interviewee: Fabrics, right?
Interviewer: What was it — what did he sell?
Interviewee: Clothes.
Interviewer: Clothes?
Interviewee: Cloth.
Interviewee: Clothes, huh?
Interviewee: Cloth, fabric.
Interviewer: Fabric, okay, yard goods.
Interviewee: Huh?
Interviewer: Does that say — yard goods.
Interviewee: Yard goods.
Interviewer: Yard goods, okay. And so did he — you had a store in your own home?
Interviewee: Yes, we had a room in our hou — store, okay, call it a store, that’s right. But he went out. He had his — he had a car in later years, and before that he had a bundle. And he went — he had — he had his business really in Bad Orb, and for *** three days in Bad Orb, and — and one and a half days in — in Neuehof.
Interviewer: Uh-huh, in Neuehof.
Interviewee: Yeah.
Interviewer: And your mother, did she ha — did she help him in this business, or did she have nothing —
Interviewee: No, no, no, she was just in the house, she was a —
Interviewee: She had the insurance business.
Interviewee: Oh, she had her own business. I forgot.
Interviewer: Oh, she had her own business, okay, what was hers?
Interviewee: Yeah *** he was — she was an insurance agent for the Akner und München Feuerversicherung.
Interviewer: Uh-huh, Akner und München Feuerversicherung.
Interviewee: Yeah.
Interviewer: So it means that the fire insurance company of Aachen and Mu-Munich.
Interviewee: Fire and theft, I suppose.
Interviewer: Okay. Of Aachen and München — Munich.
Interviewee: Akner and München.
Interviewer: Uh-huh.
Interviewee: Feuerversicherung.
Interviewer: Okay.
Interviewee: That’s a long time.
Interviewer: Can you tell me what your earliest memories are?
Interviewee: What?
Interviewer: Your earliest memories.
Interviewee: My earliest memories?
Interviewer: Memories, yeah, as a child. What is the — when you think back —
Interviewee: Somebody coming?
Interviewer: No.
Interviewee: We-hell. *** me in my early years *** I don’t know any more. With — with my girl — wi-with my friends?
Interviewer: Mm-hm.
Interviewee: We played on the street.
Interviewer: You played on the street.
Interviewee: We played.
Interviewer: Okay. Let me ask it this way then, did your mother do all the cooking and the cleaning at home as well, you know?
Interviewee: No, she had a maid.
Interviewer: She had a maid.
Interviewee: She had a maid. She did the cooking, but not the cleaning.
Interviewer: Okay. You were born in 1913.
Interviewee: Yeah.
Interviewer: And the first World War happened the next year.
Interviewee: In —
Interviewer: 19 four —
Interviewee: — 1918.
Interviewer: No, that’s when it ended.
Interviewee: Oh, that’s when it — oh, 1914.
Interviewer: That’s right. So it —
Interviewee: 1914, yeah.
Interviewer: So your first years were during the first World War. Do you remember anything, anything at all as a little child, of soldiers, of people marching down the streets, of —
Interviewee: Well, I remember we were scared of the — of the soldiers as children. You know, saw the soldiers on the streets and we were scared.
Interviewer: Of German sol — of your own German soldiers?
Interviewee: It was — I don’t know any more — no, there were some — I don’t know where they were from. They were not completely black, but they were —
Interviewee: You mean the uniforms?
Interviewee: No, the faces.
Interviewee: The faces?
Interviewer: Yeah, yeah.
Interviewee: Faces, but they were — where were they from? I don’t remember. We were scared of them.
Interviewer: Okay, were they — th-they weren’t German soldiers then, they were foreign soldiers. Oh, you didn’t know. You were little, you didn’t know.
Interviewee: They were soldiers.
Interviewer: Yeah. And your — do you remember playing with your brother when he was born, after he was born?
Interviewee: Sure, if — I remember. And how. We were fighting more than enough.
Interviewer: Oh, really?
Interviewee: And my mother always blamed me.
Interviewer: Sh — why?
Interviewee: Why, she — she blamed me, she always — her son was everything.
Interviewer: Ah.
Interviewee: Who knows?
Interviewer: Ah.
Interviewee: I don’t know any more. Well, we had a good time. We ler — we had a good living, there’s no doubt about it. Then when the times were bad, when war start, and the food was — we always had food because we lived in the country. And oh, I — when I went to school, let’s see first grade, second grade, who knows, you know? And my mother gave me five cents, or five pennies, you know, buy myself a — a roll, in order to get — I was hungry.
Interviewer: Mm-hm.
Interviewee: In order to fill my stomach up, I filled up with water. That I remember, I never forget that.
Interviewer: And — and when did you — when did you start going to school? How old were you when you started going?
Interviewee: Six years.
Interviewer: Six years. So that would have been 1919, or 1920, something like that?
Interviewee: I never thought of it, I don’t know any more.
Interviewer: Yeah. Can you tell us about your school? Do you have any memories of school?
Interviewee: Yeah, I do remember. It was okay, you know, the school was all right. We had to — we had strict teachers. One teacher, he — when we came — the boys, they had to bend over, and they got every day before school started, a good licking on the behind, and the girls had to show their hands.
Interviewer: And they got the ruler on the hands?
Interviewee: The ruler.
Interviewer: And was that because —
Interviewee: A nice stick.
Interviewer: Was that just sort of always? Just — just in case?
Interviewee: Sure. That’s how the teachers started.
Interviewer: Well, it sounds frightening.
Interviewee: Ah, well.
Interviewer: And was it — were there in — in — in Schlüchtern, was there a large Jewish community, or was it —
Interviewee: Yes, was a large Jewish community. I don’t *** but a large Jewish community, yes, it was nice.
Interviewer: Was it — were there also Gentiles living in there, or living there, or was it mostly Jewish?
Interviewee: No, mostly Gentile.
Interviewer: Mostly Gentile.
Interviewee: Mostly Gentile. Of the eight, I remember, before Hitler came, I think there were about a hundred Jews in Schlüchtern.
Interviewer: Uh-huh, a hundred.
Interviewee: Yeah.
Interviewer: A hundred. And did you have a synagogue?
Interviewee: Oh yes, a beautiful synagogue.
Interviewer: Yeah?
Interviewee: Upstairs and downstairs. Downstairs the men, upstairs the women.
Interviewer: And did your — were your parents religious?
Interviewee: Yes, they were religious.
Interviewer: And did you go to synagogue, did you —
Interviewee: Oh yes, oh yes. My grandmother would have killed me if I wouldn’t have gone.
Interviewer: Do you have memories of your grandmother?
Interviewee: Sure.
Interviewer: Whose mother was she?
Interviewee: My grandparents.
Interviewer: Yeah.
Interviewee: My mother’s — my mother’s parents, and then I have memory of my father’s parents. His father died young, he had — ah, what the hell? He had cancer of the liver, and in that time there was no medicine to give him for pain. He hanged himself.
Interviewer: Oh my.
Interviewee: Couldn’t take the pain any more, he hanged himself. But my grandmother lived a long time.
Interviewer: And how old were you — did she die when you were a teenager or something?
Interviewee: Yeah.
Interviewer: Yeah?
Interviewee: Yeah.
